Build a cost analysis and an economic case for a health information system and write a complete evaluation protocol.

syllabus.title: Foundations of health IT evaluation
topics: Why evaluate: failures, benefits and harms of health IT; the sociotechnical view
Evaluation frameworks: Donabedian structure-process-outcome, information systems success model, HOT-fit and NASSS
Evaluation questions, outcomes and measures at the system, user and patient level
Ethics of evaluation: consent, data protection and research ethics approval
Formative versus summative evaluation across the system life cycle

syllabus.title: Study designs and analysis
topics: Randomised trials: cluster and stepped-wedge designs
Quasi-experimental designs: interrupted time series, difference-in-differences and pre-post comparison
Observational designs: cohort, case-control and cross-sectional surveys
Sample size, power, bias and confounding
Analysing routine data: completeness, timeliness and accuracy in a national district health information platform
Effect sizes, confidence intervals and regression for evaluation data

syllabus.title: Usability, workflow and safety studies
topics: Heuristic evaluation and cognitive walkthrough
Think-aloud testing, task completion measures and System Usability Scale scoring
Time-and-motion studies and clinical workflow mapping
Alert fatigue, override rates and evaluation of clinical decision support
Patient safety: incident analysis for health IT, safety cases and human factors
Design and testing for low literacy, multilingual use and offline operation

syllabus.title: Qualitative and mixed methods
topics: Qualitative designs: interviews, focus groups, observation and ethnography
Sampling, saturation, interview guides and reflexivity
Thematic and framework analysis; coding and trustworthiness
Mixed-methods designs: convergent, explanatory sequential and exploratory sequential
Reporting standards for trials, quality improvement studies and qualitative research

syllabus.title: Implementation science and change management
topics: Implementation frameworks: CFIR, RE-AIM and Normalisation Process Theory
Change models: unfreeze-change-refreeze, stage-based eight-step models and ADKAR
Readiness assessment: power, connectivity, devices, skills and culture
Training, super-users and go-live strategies: big bang, phased, pilot and parallel run
Adoption, resistance and sustainability; why pilots fail to scale in African digital health
Governance, data stewardship and post-go-live support

syllabus.title: Procurement, vendor selection and contracting
topics: Needs specification, requests for information and requests for proposal
Open source versus commercial systems; total cost of ownership and vendor lock-in
Scoring vendors: weighted criteria, scripted demonstrations and reference checks
Contracts and service levels: licensing, support, data ownership and exit clauses
Public procurement rules and donor-funded projects

syllabus.title: Organisational behaviour and project leadership
topics: Project management for health IT: scope, schedule, risk, Gantt charts and the critical path
Leadership, clinical champions and stakeholder management
Organisational culture, power and communication in hospitals
Managing risks and issues; analysing project failure
Migrating legacy records: data mapping, cleansing, reconciliation and cut-over
Benefits realisation management

syllabus.title: Health economics and return on investment
topics: Cost analysis: capital, recurrent and hidden costs; total cost of ownership
Cost-effectiveness, cost-benefit and cost-utility analysis; QALY and DALY
Return on investment, net present value, payback period and sensitivity analysis
Budget impact and financing: national insurance and donor funding
Value for money and equity in low-resource settings

syllabus.title: Evaluation project
topics: Writing an evaluation protocol: aims, design, outcomes and ethics
Data collection and analysis plans
Reporting and feeding results back to decision makers
Defending an evaluation: peer review, limitations and next steps

courses.title: Financial Econometrics and Quantitative Methods
topics: Regression and time-series models
Volatility and risk models
Estimation and hypothesis testing in finance
Cointegration and long-run relationships
Panel data and event studies
Monte Carlo and bootstrap methods
Backtesting and model validation
courses.description: Statistical and econometric methods for financial data at graduate level: regression, time series, volatility and risk models, cointegration, panel data, event studies, simulation and model validation. Students estimate and test models on market and macroeconomic series in the maths lab and in R or Python, and finish by replicating and extending an empirical finance result.
modelledOn: Brooks, Introductory Econometrics for Finance
Tsay, Analysis of Financial Time Series
Campbell, Lo and MacKinlay, The Econometrics of Financial Markets
outcomes: Describe the stylised facts of financial returns and test distributional assumptions with appropriate statistics.
Estimate regression models with robust standard errors and instruments, and interpret asset pricing regressions.
Identify, estimate and forecast with ARMA, VAR and GARCH-family models and evaluate forecasts out of sample.
Test for unit roots and cointegration and build error-correction models for long-run relationships.
Run event studies and panel regressions with correct inference, and use Monte Carlo and bootstrap methods to check test properties.
Backtest and validate risk and forecasting models, and report the limits of a model clearly.

syllabus.title: Statistical foundations for financial data
topics: Simple and log returns; stylised facts: fat tails, volatility clustering, skewness and leverage effect
Return distributions: normal, Student t and stable laws; QQ plots and the Jarque-Bera test
Estimation: method of moments and maximum likelihood; consistency, efficiency and standard errors
Hypothesis testing: size, power, p-values and the multiple-testing problem
Matrix algebra for regression and asymptotic theory in brief: law of large numbers and central limit theorem

syllabus.title: Regression models and asset pricing
topics: Ordinary least squares: assumptions, Gauss-Markov theorem and inference
Heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation: White and Newey-West standard errors, generalised least squares
Endogeneity, instrumental variables and two-stage least squares
Asset pricing regressions: CAPM, Fama-French factors and Fama-MacBeth cross-sectional tests
Model selection and multicollinearity: information criteria, ridge and lasso

syllabus.title: Time-series models
topics: Stationarity, autocorrelation and partial autocorrelation functions, and unit root tests (ADF, KPSS)
ARMA models and Box-Jenkins identification, estimation and diagnostics
Forecasting and forecast evaluation: RMSE, MAE and the Diebold-Mariano test
Vector autoregressions: Granger causality and impulse response functions
Structural breaks and regime-switching models

syllabus.title: Volatility and risk models
topics: Realised volatility, rolling windows and exponentially weighted moving averages
ARCH and GARCH: specification, estimation by maximum likelihood, asymmetric extensions (GJR, EGARCH)
Multivariate volatility: conditional correlation models and covariance forecasting
Value at Risk and expected shortfall: historical, parametric and filtered historical simulation
Extreme value theory: block maxima, peaks over threshold and tail index estimation

syllabus.title: Cointegration and long-run relationships
topics: Spurious regression and the Granger representation
Engle-Granger two-step test and residual-based cointegration
Johansen procedure: rank tests and vector error-correction models
Error correction in practice: pairs spreads, exchange rates and purchasing power parity
Application: commodity prices, the cedi and inflation in Ghana as a cointegration study

syllabus.title: Panel data and event studies
topics: Pooled, fixed-effects and random-effects panel models; the Hausman test
Clustered standard errors and cross-sectional dependence
Difference-in-differences and policy evaluation, such as the effect of a mobile money levy
Event-study methodology: market model, abnormal and cumulative abnormal returns, test statistics
Testing market efficiency: variance ratios, predictability and anomalies

syllabus.title: Monte Carlo and bootstrap methods
topics: Simulating asset paths: geometric Brownian motion, GARCH and jump models; antithetic variates
The bootstrap: iid, residual, block and stationary bootstrap
Monte Carlo studies of size and power of tests and of estimator bias
Simulation-based risk: scenario generation for Value at Risk and stress testing
Reproducible computational workflow: seeds, version control and documented code

syllabus.title: Backtesting, validation and project
topics: Backtesting Value at Risk: Kupiec, Christoffersen and traffic-light tests
Out-of-sample evaluation, rolling windows and the model confidence set
Data snooping and reality checks: White reality check and superior predictive ability
Model risk, validation reports and governance
Project: replicate and extend a published empirical finance result, with a full robustness section

courses.title: Financial Risk Management
topics: Market risk and value at risk
Credit risk and scoring models
Liquidity and operational risk
Stress testing and scenario analysis
Counterparty risk and collateral
Model risk and validation
Regulatory capital and risk reporting
courses.description: How banks, microfinance institutions and fintech firms measure and control market, credit, liquidity, operational, counterparty and model risk. Students estimate value at risk, build credit scorecards, run stress tests and produce a regulatory-style risk report on portfolios drawn from Ghanaian and regional markets.
modelledOn: Hull, Risk Management and Financial Institutions
McNeil, Frey and Embrechts, Quantitative Risk Management
Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, Basel Framework standards
Jorion, Value at Risk: The New Benchmark for Managing Financial Risk
outcomes: Compute and backtest value at risk and expected shortfall with parametric, historical and Monte Carlo methods.
Build and validate a credit scorecard and estimate expected and unexpected credit loss for a loan portfolio.
Model liquidity and operational loss exposures, including mobile-money float and fraud scenarios.
Design macroeconomic stress scenarios and translate them into portfolio losses and capital impact.
Quantify counterparty exposure and the effect of netting and collateral.
Assess model risk and prepare a risk report that links measured risk to regulatory capital.

syllabus.title: Risk foundations and measures
topics: Risk taxonomy: market, credit, liquidity, operational, counterparty and model risk; risk versus uncertainty
Returns and stylised facts: log returns, volatility clustering and fat tails
Risk measures: variance, value at risk, expected shortfall and the coherence axioms
Risk governance: three lines of defence, risk appetite and limits

syllabus.title: Market risk
topics: Parametric (delta-normal) value at risk and the variance-covariance method
Historical simulation, filtered historical simulation and Monte Carlo value at risk
Volatility models: EWMA and GARCH(1,1)
Extreme value theory: peaks over threshold and the generalised Pareto tail
Backtesting: Kupiec proportion-of-failures test, Christoffersen independence test and the traffic-light approach
Portfolio risk: factor models, marginal and component value at risk, and exchange-rate exposure to the cedi
Interest rate risk: duration, convexity, DV01 and key rate durations

syllabus.title: Credit risk
topics: Probability of default, loss given default and exposure at default; expected and unexpected loss
Scorecards: logistic regression, weight of evidence, information value, Gini and KS statistics for microloans
Structural (Merton) and reduced-form models of default
Portfolio credit risk: the Vasicek single-factor model, default correlation and credit value at risk
IFRS 9 expected credit loss: staging and forward-looking provisions
Rating migration matrices and Markov chain transition models

syllabus.title: Liquidity and operational risk
topics: Funding and market liquidity: bid-ask costs, liquidity-adjusted value at risk, liquidity coverage and net stable funding ratios
Runs and float risk in mobile money and savings institutions
Operational risk: the loss distribution approach with frequency and severity models
Fraud and cyber loss scenarios and key risk indicators
Business continuity, incident response and risk transfer through insurance

syllabus.title: Stress testing and scenario analysis
topics: Sensitivity analysis, scenario analysis and reverse stress testing
Macroeconomic scenario design: commodity prices for cocoa, gold and oil, currency depreciation and rate shocks
Satellite models linking macroeconomic variables to default rates and losses
Governance of stress tests: management actions, documentation and board challenge
Case study: sovereign debt restructuring and its effect on bank balance sheets

syllabus.title: Counterparty risk and collateral
topics: Exposure profiles: expected exposure, potential future exposure and expected positive exposure
Credit valuation adjustment and wrong-way risk
Netting, close-out and master agreements
Collateral and margin: variation and initial margin, haircuts and central counterparties
Settlement risk and payment systems

syllabus.title: Model risk and validation
topics: Sources of model risk: specification, estimation, implementation and use
Validation practice: conceptual soundness, outcome analysis, benchmarking and back-testing
Model inventory, tiering, documentation and governance
Parameter uncertainty and model averaging
Machine learning in risk models: explainability, drift and challenger models
Case studies of model failures and the lessons for governance

syllabus.title: Regulatory capital and risk reporting
topics: The Basel framework: three pillars, capital ratios and risk-weighted assets
Standardised and internal ratings-based approaches, the Vasicek capital formula and the fundamental review of the trading book
Prudential requirements of the central bank in Ghana and the region, and how local rules differ from Basel
ICAAP, risk dashboards and board reporting
Capstone: a risk report for a bank or microfinance loan and trading portfolio

courses.title: Foundations of Biomedical and Health Informatics
topics: Definitions, history and scope of the field
Clinical data, information and knowledge
Health records and information systems
Standards, terminologies and interoperability
Decision support and artificial intelligence
Public health, consumer and research informatics
Privacy, security and ethics
courses.description: The core ideas of biomedical and health informatics: how clinical data becomes information and knowledge, how records and standards move it between systems, and how decision support, public health and research use it. In the lab students work through clinical and policy scenarios and build small databases, queries and exchange messages.
modelledOn: Shortliffe and Cimino (eds.), Biomedical Informatics: Computer Applications in Health Care and Biomedicine
Hersh, Health Informatics: Practical Guide
HL7 FHIR specification and ISO/TC 215 health informatics standards
WHO, Global Strategy on Digital Health
outcomes: Define the scope of biomedical and health informatics and place real activities within its sub-fields.
Describe how clinical data is captured, coded, stored and quality-checked in health information systems.
Use terminologies and exchange standards such as ICD, SNOMED CT, HL7 v2 and FHIR to represent and move clinical information.
Evaluate clinical decision support and predictive models for validity, safety and fairness.
Apply privacy law, security controls and ethical frameworks to health data decisions.
Plan, procure and evaluate a digital health intervention for a resource-limited district.

syllabus.title: The field: scope, history and health systems
topics: Definitions and sub-fields: biomedical, clinical, public health, consumer and translational informatics
History: from paper records and literature databases to electronic records, expert systems and genomics
Health systems and their information needs: primary care compounds, referral, insurance and Ghana's routine reporting systems
Informatics roles and competencies: clinical informatics lead, health data analyst, interoperability engineer
Socio-technical view of health IT and why implementations fail
Global digital health strategy and the burden of disease in Africa

syllabus.title: Clinical data, information and knowledge
topics: Data, information, knowledge and wisdom; data types: structured, free text, images, signals, genomic and patient-generated
The clinical encounter and workflow; problem-oriented and SOAP notes
Data quality: completeness, accuracy, timeliness, missingness and bias
Clinical coding practice: ICD-10, ICD-11 and procedure codes
Test performance for informaticians: sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, ROC and prevalence effects
Evidence sources: guidelines, evidence-based medicine and systematic reviews

syllabus.title: Health records and information systems
topics: Electronic health record architecture: patient index, orders, results, documentation and pharmacy
Open-source and low-resource systems for records and aggregate reporting, such as OpenMRS and DHIS2
Departmental systems (laboratory, imaging, pharmacy) and patient identity matching
Usability, human factors, alert fatigue and workflow redesign
Implementation and change management: training, go-live, downtime procedures and rollback
Clinical data modelling in relational databases: encounters, observations and patient timelines
Routine health information systems: facility reporting, indicators, data warehouses and dashboards

syllabus.title: Standards, terminologies and interoperability
topics: Terminologies: SNOMED CT, LOINC, RxNorm and UMLS; mapping local terms
HL7 version 2 messages and segments; clinical document architecture
FHIR: resources, REST API, profiles, bundles and SMART apps
DICOM, IHE profiles and openEHR archetypes
Interoperability levels, health information exchange and national architecture; patient matching
Ontologies and knowledge graphs in biomedicine

syllabus.title: Decision support and artificial intelligence
topics: Clinical decision support: rules, alerts, order sets and the five rights
Probabilistic reasoning: Bayesian diagnosis, likelihood ratios, decision trees and utilities
Machine learning for clinical prediction: risk scores, validation, calibration and fairness
Natural language processing, imaging AI and large language models in clinical settings: errors and safety
Regulation, local validation and dataset shift for imported models
Explainability and clinician trust

syllabus.title: Public health, consumer and research informatics
topics: Surveillance: notifiable disease reporting, syndromic surveillance, epidemic curves and outbreak detection
Mobile health: community health workers, SMS and USSD, telemedicine and wearables
Consumer informatics: patient portals, health literacy and personal records
Research informatics: trial data management, electronic case report forms, CDISC and common data models
Translational informatics and genomic medicine
Health economics of digital interventions: cost-effectiveness and budget impact

syllabus.title: Privacy, security and ethics
topics: Privacy law and consent: Ghana's Data Protection Act, HIPAA and GDPR compared
Security controls: role-based access, audit trails, break-glass access and encryption
De-identification: k-anonymity and its limits for small populations
Ethical frameworks: autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence and justice; data sovereignty and community consent
Breach response, risk assessment and cross-border data
Equity, the digital divide and inclusive design

syllabus.title: Strategy, procurement and evaluation
topics: Digital health strategy, governance and decision rights
Enterprise architecture and maturity models for health information exchange
Procurement and vendor selection with weighted criteria
Sustainability, donor funding and handover to national ownership
Evaluating health IT: pragmatic and stepped-wedge trials, usability scales and cost-effectiveness
Capstone: an informatics solution for a district with weak connectivity

courses.title: Generative AI and Large Language Models
topics: Language model pre-training
Instruction tuning and alignment
Prompting, retrieval and tool use
Diffusion and multimodal generation
Evaluation and benchmarking
Serving, cost and efficiency
Safety, misuse and governance
courses.description: How large language models and diffusion models are built, aligned, evaluated, served and governed, taught with the maths and the engineering at graduate depth. Students implement small transformers and samplers, build retrieval and tool-using systems, evaluate them and cost their deployment in the browser lab.
modelledOn: Jurafsky and Martin, Speech and Language Processing (transformer and large language model chapters)
Goodfellow, Bengio and Courville, Deep Learning
The original transformer paper (Attention Is All You Need) and the scaling-law and alignment research literature
Huyen, Designing Machine Learning Systems
outcomes: Implement a small decoder-only transformer with tokenisation, attention and sampling, and explain each component mathematically.
Explain pre-training data, scaling laws and distributed training, and estimate the compute needed for a given model and dataset.
Apply supervised fine-tuning, parameter-efficient adaptation and preference optimisation, and describe their failure modes.
Design retrieval-augmented and tool-using systems and measure their accuracy, grounding and robustness to prompt injection.
Evaluate generative models with benchmarks, judges and human studies, and report uncertainty and contamination risks.
Cost, optimise and govern the deployment of a model, including safety evaluation, misuse risks and regulatory duties.

syllabus.title: Language models and the transformer
topics: Language modelling: n-grams, cross-entropy and perplexity
Tokenisation: byte-pair encoding, SentencePiece and the token cost of Twi, Ewe and Hausa text
Self-attention and the transformer: multi-head attention, rotary position encodings and layer normalisation
Decoder-only models: the causal mask, the next-token objective and the key-value cache
Decoding: greedy, beam, temperature, top-k and nucleus sampling; constrained and structured decoding

syllabus.title: Pre-training at scale
topics: Data pipelines: crawling, deduplication, quality filtering, licensing and consent, low-resource languages
Scaling laws: compute-optimal training and the debate over emergent abilities
Optimisation: AdamW, learning rate schedules, mixed precision, gradient clipping and loss spikes
Distributed training: data, tensor and pipeline parallelism, ZeRO and fully sharded training
Mixture-of-experts, state-space models and other alternatives to dense attention

syllabus.title: Instruction tuning and alignment
topics: Supervised fine-tuning on instruction data and chat templates
Parameter-efficient fine-tuning: LoRA, QLoRA and adapters
Reinforcement learning from human feedback: Bradley-Terry reward models and PPO
Direct preference optimisation, learning from AI feedback and constitutional methods; reward hacking and sycophancy
Reasoning models: chain of thought, verifier-based reinforcement learning and test-time compute

syllabus.title: Prompting, retrieval and tool use
topics: In-context learning: few-shot prompting, chain of thought and self-consistency
Embeddings and vector search: dense retrieval, HNSW approximate nearest neighbours and chunking
Retrieval-augmented generation: pipeline design, reranking, citations and failure modes
Tool use and function calling: JSON schemas, the ReAct loop and multi-step planning
Agents in practice: memory, long-context limits, context engineering and prompt injection

syllabus.title: Diffusion and multimodal generation
topics: Generative model families: autoregressive models, VAEs, GANs and normalising flows
Diffusion models: forward noising, denoising score matching, DDPM sampling and classifier-free guidance
Latent diffusion and text conditioning by cross-attention
Vision-language models and CLIP contrastive pre-training; speech recognition and synthesis
Video and audio generation, synthetic data and watermarking

syllabus.title: Evaluation and benchmarking
topics: Intrinsic and extrinsic evaluation: perplexity, BLEU and ROUGE and their limits
Benchmarks for knowledge, reasoning and code (pass@k); contamination and saturation
LLM-as-judge and human preference arenas; inter-annotator agreement and judge bias
Hallucination and factuality measurement; calibration of confidence
Evaluating for local languages and tasks; statistical significance and confidence intervals

syllabus.title: Serving, cost and efficiency
topics: Inference mechanics: prefill and decode, memory-bound decoding, KV-cache size, continuous batching and paged attention
Quantisation (int8, int4, GPTQ and AWQ), pruning and distillation
Speculative decoding, FlashAttention and tensor-parallel serving
Cost modelling: tokens, GPU hours and utilisation; cloud versus on-device; autoscaling endpoints
Small models at the edge: phones, low bandwidth and offline use

syllabus.title: Safety, misuse and governance
topics: Harms: bias, toxicity, privacy leakage, memorisation and copyright
Adversarial behaviour: jailbreaks, prompt injection, data poisoning and red-teaming
Misuse: disinformation, fraud and deepfakes; watermarking and content provenance
Governance: AI regulation, model cards, audits and responsible release; the African Union data and AI strategies
Project: build and evaluate a retrieval-augmented assistant for farmer advisory or health information

courses.title: Graduate Game Project
topics: Concept pitch and scope control
Studio team roles and pipelines
Iterative prototyping
Playtesting and telemetry review
Vertical slice and milestone reviews
Release preparation and postmortem
Technical report and portfolio
courses.description: A studio-style team project in which students take a game from pitch to vertical slice to release candidate, run playtests, read telemetry and write a postmortem. In the lab they work through branching production cases, plan schedules and risks, and analyse test data.
modelledOn: Schell, The Art of Game Design: A Book of Lenses
Fullerton, Game Design Workshop
Bethke, Game Development and Production
Game Accessibility Guidelines (community standard) and the postmortem format used in game industry magazines
outcomes: Write a concept pitch and scope plan with pillars, a cut list and a risk register for a game aimed at a stated audience.
Organise a team with clear roles, a sprint process and a version-controlled production pipeline.
Plan and run iterative prototypes and playtests, and turn observations and telemetry into design changes.
Define and deliver a vertical slice and pass milestone reviews against stated quality criteria.
Prepare a game for release with a quality, localisation and store-readiness checklist.
Write a postmortem, a technical report and a portfolio piece that record the project honestly and show individual contribution.

syllabus.title: Concept pitch and scope control
topics: High concept, design pillars, target audience and a one-page pitch
Players and platforms in Ghana and West Africa: low-end Android, data costs, mobile money and offline play
Scope control: MoSCoW priorities, the cut list and feature freeze
Business models and monetisation: premium, ad-supported, in-app purchase and the ethics of each
Risk register, feasibility study and the game design document as a living document

syllabus.title: Studio team roles and pipelines
topics: Roles: producer, designer, programmer, artist, audio, QA and community; how responsibilities overlap in a small team
Agile for games: sprints, backlogs, kanban boards, stand-ups and retrospectives
Production pipeline: version control for code and art, build automation and naming conventions
Team charter, communication with unreliable connectivity and resolving conflict
Estimating tasks and planning milestones with Gantt charts and critical path

syllabus.title: Iterative prototyping
topics: Paper prototypes and greyboxing to test mechanics before art
Core loop analysis and the MDA framework of mechanics, dynamics and aesthetics
Throwaway prototypes versus evolutionary prototypes; deciding what to keep
Game feel and feedback: timing, animation, sound and screen response
Technical risk spikes: testing the hardest feature first

syllabus.title: Playtesting and telemetry review
topics: Planning a playtest: goals, recruiting players, protocol and consent
Observation and questionnaires: think-aloud, interviews, usability scales and engagement surveys
Telemetry design: event schema, funnels, retention at day 1 and day 7, and privacy limits
Reading data to balance difficulty and economy, and detecting where players quit
Accessibility and inclusive design testing: colour, controls, text size and cognitive load

syllabus.title: Vertical slice and milestone reviews
topics: Milestone ladder: concept, first playable, vertical slice, alpha, beta, release candidate
Defining the vertical slice and setting its quality bar
Running a milestone review: demo, metrics, risks and decisions to continue, cut or cancel
Sustainable pace: avoiding crunch, burn-down charts and cutting scope early
Integration, build stability and keeping the game always playable

syllabus.title: Quality, localisation and platform readiness
topics: QA process: test plans, bug reporting, severity and priority, and triage meetings
Compatibility and performance on target devices, including low-memory phones
Localisation and internationalisation: English, French, Twi, Hausa and right-to-left text
Legal matters: licences for engines and assets, music rights, age ratings and children's data
Store listing, compliance checks and payment integration

syllabus.title: Release preparation and postmortem
topics: Launch plan: store page, trailer, press kit, community channels and soft launch
Live operations: patching, event calendars and handling player support
Success metrics: downloads, retention, revenue per user and review scores
The postmortem format: what went right, what went wrong and what to change
Handling a failed launch, a critical bug or a negative public reaction

syllabus.title: Technical report and portfolio
topics: Structure of a technical report: problem, design decisions, implementation, evaluation, limitations
Portfolio pieces: playable build, gameplay video, design breakdowns and a case study
Individual contribution statements and fair peer assessment
Final showcase: presenting to a panel and answering critical questions
Career pathways in African and global game studios, freelancing and funding

courses.title: Graduate Research Methods
topics: Formulating research questions
Literature search and critical reading
Experimental design and reproducibility
Statistical evidence and reporting
Research ethics and integrity
Academic writing and peer review
Presenting and defending research
courses.description: A field-neutral course on how to plan, run, report and defend research in any computing discipline: turning a topic into a question, reading the literature, designing reproducible experiments, handling statistical evidence, working ethically, and writing and presenting results. Students practise on ethics scenarios, computational notebooks and a research proposal they develop through the term.
modelledOn: Booth, Colomb and Williams, The Craft of Research
Wohlin, Runeson, Host, Ohlsson, Regnell and Wesslen, Experimentation in Software Engineering
Wasserman, All of Statistics
Committee on Publication Ethics guidelines and the Singapore Statement on Research Integrity
outcomes: Formulate a focused, answerable and ethical research question with testable hypotheses in a chosen computing field.
Search, read and critically appraise the literature and synthesise it to justify a research gap.
Design a controlled, reproducible study and identify its threats to validity.
Analyse data with appropriate statistics, quantify uncertainty and report results honestly.
Identify ethical issues in a study, obtain the right approvals and protect participants and data.
Write a research proposal and a paper section, review a peer's work, and present and defend a project.

syllabus.title: Research questions and design
topics: Kinds of research in computing: empirical, theoretical, design science and engineering
From topic to question: narrowing, feasibility and significance
Hypotheses, claims, falsifiability and kinds of contribution
Operationalising constructs: variables, metrics and measurement validity
Choosing a design: quantitative, qualitative and mixed methods
Scoping with real constraints: data access, compute, time and local context

syllabus.title: Literature search and critical reading
topics: Search strategy: databases, keywords, Boolean queries and citation chasing
Narrative and systematic reviews; the PRISMA flow diagram
Reading a paper in three passes; appraisal checklists
Synthesis: concept matrices, themes and identifying a gap
Reference managers, citation styles and avoiding plagiarism
Judging sources: predatory venues, preprints and retractions

syllabus.title: Experimental design and reproducibility
topics: Controlled experiments: baselines, controls and ablations
Sampling, randomisation, blocking and confounds
Threats to validity: internal, external, construct and conclusion
Reproducibility and replicability: seeds, environments and containers
Data and code management: version control, notebooks, documentation and FAIR data
Benchmarks, measurement error and simulation studies

syllabus.title: Statistical evidence and reporting
topics: Descriptive statistics, distributions, outliers and honest graphics
Estimation, standard errors, confidence intervals and the bootstrap
Hypothesis tests, p-values, power and sample size
Effect sizes and multiple comparisons: family-wise error and false discovery rate
Non-parametric tests and comparing systems across datasets
Regression models and a Bayesian summary of evidence
Reporting pitfalls: p-hacking, selective reporting, and the garden of forking paths

syllabus.title: Qualitative and mixed methods
topics: Surveys: questionnaire design, sampling frames and response bias
Interviews and focus groups, including with low-literacy participants
Thematic analysis, coding and inter-rater agreement
Case studies and evaluating a designed artefact
User studies and usability evaluation

syllabus.title: Research ethics and integrity
topics: Core principles: respect for persons, beneficence and justice; informed consent
Ethics review boards and approval processes; working in Ghana and across Africa
Misconduct: fabrication, falsification, plagiarism and questionable practices
Conflicts of interest, authorship and credit; dual-use and responsible technology
Community engagement, benefit sharing and avoiding extractive research
Data protection, anonymisation and the secure handling of research data

syllabus.title: Academic writing, proposals and peer review
topics: The structure of a paper: introduction, method, results and discussion
Abstracts, claims and related work
Figures, tables and clear reporting of results
The peer review process: writing a review and responding to reviewers
Publishing: venues, open access, preprints and author contributions
Writing a research proposal: aims, plan, timeline and budget

syllabus.title: Presenting and defending research
topics: Structuring a talk and its slides
Posters and lightning talks
Handling questions and defending design choices
Planning a thesis: supervision, milestones and time management

courses.title: Hardware Accelerators and Custom Computing
topics: GPU architecture and programming
FPGA acceleration flows
Dataflow and systolic designs
Machine learning accelerators
High-level synthesis
Memory bandwidth and roofline models
Energy-efficient design
courses.description: Why and how computation is moved from general processors onto GPUs, FPGAs and custom dataflow hardware. Students model speedups, reason about memory bandwidth with roofline plots, build pipelined and systolic circuits in the circuit bench, run kernels on a GPU model and measure energy on small boards.
modelledOn: Hennessy and Patterson, Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach
Kirk and Hwu, Programming Massively Parallel Processors
Sze, Chen, Yang and Emer, Efficient Processing of Deep Neural Networks
Hauck and DeHon, Reconfigurable Computing
outcomes: Predict the benefit of acceleration using Amdahl's law, offload costs and performance-per-watt metrics.
Write and optimise GPU kernels reasoning about warps, memory coalescing, shared memory and occupancy.
Design pipelined, dataflow and systolic circuits and explain the FPGA flow from RTL or high-level synthesis to timing closure.
Map neural network layers onto accelerator dataflows and evaluate the effect of quantisation and sparsity.
Use roofline and energy models to locate bottlenecks and justify design decisions quantitatively.
Deliver an accelerated kernel with a baseline comparison, a design-space exploration and a written evaluation.

syllabus.title: The case for acceleration

syllabus.title: GPU architecture and programming

syllabus.title: FPGA acceleration flows

Stream processing with FIFOs and backpressure
Coarse-grained reconfigurable arrays and spatial architectures

syllabus.title: Machine learning accelerators

Edge inference on microcontrollers and low-power neural processors for off-grid devices

syllabus.title: Memory bandwidth and roofline models

syllabus.title: Energy-efficient design
topics: CMOS power: dynamic, short-circuit and leakage power; P = C V squared f

syllabus.title: Project: accelerating a kernel

Project presentation and review

courses.title: Human-Robot Interaction

Interaction design for robots
Teleoperation and shared autonomy
Social robots
Study design with human participants

Evaluation metrics
courses.description: A graduate course on how people work, live and communicate with robots, covering trust, interaction design, teleoperation, social robots, safety and the design of studies with human participants. Students model interaction flows in the diagram studio and make design, ethics and study decisions in scored scenarios.
modelledOn: Goodrich and Schultz, Human-Robot Interaction: A Survey
Bartneck et al., Human-Robot Interaction: An Introduction
Lazar, Feng and Hochheiser, Research Methods in Human-Computer Interaction
ISO 10218 and ISO/TS 15066 on collaborative robot safety
outcomes: Analyse an interaction scenario in terms of human factors, workload, trust and levels of autonomy.
Design and document multimodal robot interactions, including dialogue, motion legibility and accessibility needs.
Specify a teleoperation or shared-autonomy architecture that copes with latency and weak networks.
Plan a human-participant study with hypotheses, design, sample size, consent and analysis.
Carry out a hazard and ethics review of a robot deployment in a health, farm or factory setting.
Select and justify evaluation metrics, and critique published HRI studies.

syllabus.title: Foundations of human-robot interaction
topics: Scope of HRI: roles of operator, collaborator, bystander and supervisor
Robot types and levels of autonomy
Human perception, attention, workload and situation awareness
Mental models and anthropomorphism

syllabus.title: Human factors and trust

Measuring trust: questionnaires and behavioural measures
Transparency, explanation, legibility and predictability
Failure, apology and trust repair
Workload measurement with NASA-TLX
Automation bias and complacency

syllabus.title: Interaction design for robots

Dialogue and multimodal interfaces; low-resource languages such as Twi, Ewe and Hausa
Behaviour design: motion legibility, proxemics, lights and sounds

Accessibility and inclusive design

syllabus.title: Teleoperation and shared autonomy

IT and organisational change

courses.description: A graduate seminar on the theories that explain how information systems are built, adopted and transform organisations and societies. Students read and critique foundational theory, model systems and ecosystems in diagrams, argue positions in branching case studies, and develop a theory-grounded research proposal on an African digital innovation.
modelledOn: Laudon and Laudon, Management Information Systems
Rogers, Diffusion of Innovations
Hevner, March, Park and Ram, Design Science in Information Systems Research
Association for Information Systems, curriculum guidelines for graduate information systems programmes
outcomes: Explain the core subject matter of information systems and the main philosophical and methodological positions used to study it.
Analyse a case through socio-technical, structuration and affordance lenses and justify the choice of lens.
Apply and critique adoption theories (diffusion, TAM, UTAUT, task-technology fit) and design a survey instrument to test one.
Model a digital innovation or platform ecosystem in terms of layered architecture, generativity, boundary resources and governance.
Evaluate how IT changes organisations and societies, using evidence on value, change management, inequality and sustainability.
Write a research proposal that poses a question, positions it in the literature, and chooses a justified method.

syllabus.title: Foundations of the IS discipline
topics: The identity of the field: the IT artefact, its context and its relation to computer science and management

syllabus.title: Socio-technical systems

Structuration theory and the appropriation of technology in use

syllabus.title: Research seminar: proposal and critique
topics: Forming a research question and positioning it in the literature

distributed file systems and column stores

cluster resource managers

courses.description: How data is stored, processed, streamed and served across clusters, from MapReduce to feature stores. Students write dataflow jobs, run cluster experiments in the cloud console, tune queries on the database engine and benchmark systems with proper methodology.
modelledOn: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications
Karau, Konwinski, Wendell and Zaharia, Learning Spark
The original MapReduce and Google File System research papers
outcomes: Express batch analytics as MapReduce and dataflow jobs and reason about shuffle cost, skew and fault recovery.
Choose file formats, storage engines and partitioning schemes for a given access pattern.
Build stream processing pipelines with correct windowing, state and delivery semantics.
Explain cluster resource management, data-parallel training and feature store design for machine learning platforms.
Design and run a sound benchmark and use scalability laws and cost models to justify an architecture.

Project report and architecture defence

courses.description: Machine learning methods for clinical data and the specific ways that health data defeats naive modelling: missing and biased records, irregular signals, causal questions, subgroup harm and dataset shift. Students build and evaluate clinical risk models, signal and text pipelines and causal analyses in notebooks, then judge regulation and deployment in Ghanaian and wider African health settings.
modelledOn: Hastie, Tibshirani and Friedman, The Elements of Statistical Learning
Hernan and Robins, Causal Inference: What If
Steyerberg, Clinical Prediction Models
WHO guidance on ethics and governance of artificial intelligence for health
outcomes: Prepare clinical records for modelling, naming the sources of missingness, bias and label error and choosing sound cohort definitions.
Build and evaluate risk and survival models with discrimination, calibration and decision-curve analysis on a time-respecting split.
Process physiological signals, medical images and clinical text with appropriate models and judge their failure modes.
Estimate treatment effects from observational data using propensity, doubly robust and target-trial approaches, and state the assumptions required.
Audit a model for subgroup performance, dataset shift and uncertainty, and design monitoring for it after deployment.
Assess a clinical AI product against regulatory, validation and ethical requirements and plan its deployment in a low-resource health system.

Irregular sampling, measurement bias and why a lab test being ordered is itself a signal
Selection and time-related biases: immortal time, leakage and look-ahead

Discrimination: ROC and precision-recall analysis, and their dependence on prevalence

courses.description: The theory behind statistical inference: probability foundations, optimal estimation, likelihood and Bayes methods, hypothesis testing, asymptotics, high-dimensional statistics and non-parametric methods. Students prove core results on paper and then test them with simulation studies in the maths lab and code runner.

Lehmann and Casella, Theory of Point Estimation
van der Vaart, Asymptotic Statistics
Wainwright, High-Dimensional Statistics: A Non-Asymptotic Viewpoint

Derive sufficient statistics, optimal unbiased estimators and information bounds for standard models.
Construct maximum likelihood and Bayes estimators, compute them numerically and compare them under a loss function.
Derive most powerful and likelihood-based tests and confidence regions, and prove their error properties.
Establish consistency and asymptotic normality of estimators, including under model misspecification.
Analyse high-dimensional and non-parametric procedures with concentration inequalities and verify claims by simulation.

Minimax lower bounds: Le Cam and Fano methods

Implement negotiation, task-allocation and argumentation protocols for cooperating software agents.
Train and evaluate agents in multi-agent reinforcement learning settings, and explain failures such as non-stationarity and social dilemmas.
Simulate collective behaviour and critique recent multi-agent research with respect to evaluation, robustness and ethics.

syllabus.title: Agents and rational choice
topics: Agent architectures: reactive, deliberative, BDI and layered
Utility theory: preferences, the von Neumann-Morgenstern axioms and risk attitudes
Environment properties and multi-agent settings
Decision-theoretic agents: expected utility and Markov decision processes
Agent communication: speech acts, FIPA-ACL and ontologies

syllabus.title: Normal-form games
topics: Strategic games, dominance and iterated elimination of dominated strategies
Nash equilibrium and best response; existence by fixed-point theorems
Mixed strategies, support enumeration and the Lemke-Howson algorithm for bimatrix games
Zero-sum games, the minimax theorem and its LP formulation
Correlated and coarse correlated equilibrium; price of anarchy
Classic games: prisoner's dilemma, stag hunt, chicken and battle of the sexes

syllabus.title: Extensive-form, repeated and evolutionary games
topics: Game trees, perfect and imperfect information and information sets
Backward induction and subgame-perfect equilibrium; minimax with alpha-beta pruning
Sequence-form representation and Bayesian games; Bayes-Nash equilibrium
Repeated games: the folk theorem, grim trigger, tit-for-tat and discounting
Evolutionary game theory: evolutionarily stable strategies and replicator dynamics
Learning in games: fictitious play, regret matching and convergence to coarse correlated equilibrium

syllabus.title: Mechanism design
topics: Social choice, dominant-strategy incentive compatibility and the revelation principle
The VCG mechanism, Clarke pivot rule and Groves mechanisms
Optimal mechanisms: virtual valuations and revenue maximisation
Impossibility results: Arrow's theorem and the Gibbard-Satterthwaite theorem
Budget balance, individual rationality and algorithmic mechanism design

syllabus.title: Auctions, voting and matching
topics: Auction formats: English, Dutch, first-price and second-price; revenue equivalence
Bidding equilibria; private versus common values and the winner's curse
Combinatorial and multi-unit auctions; winner determination and spectrum auctions
Voting rules: plurality, Borda, Condorcet methods, approval and single transferable vote; manipulation
Matching markets: stable matching and the Gale-Shapley algorithm; school and organ allocation
Cooperative games and fair division: the core, the Shapley value and bargaining

syllabus.title: Coordination, negotiation and argumentation
topics: Coordination: conventions, focal points, social laws and task allocation by contract net
Distributed constraint optimisation: ADOPT and DPOP
Negotiation: alternating-offers bargaining, monotonic concession protocol and automated negotiation strategies
Argumentation: abstract argumentation frameworks, grounded and preferred semantics and dialogue games
Coalition formation and teamwork with joint intentions

syllabus.title: Multi-agent reinforcement learning
topics: Stochastic games and MARL settings: cooperative, competitive and mixed
Independent Q-learning and the non-stationarity problem
Centralised training with decentralised execution: MADDPG and QMIX value decomposition
Self-play, population-based training and opponent modelling
Learning to communicate and emergent protocols
Credit assignment and sequential social dilemmas

syllabus.title: Swarm and collective behaviour
topics: Flocking, consensus protocols and convergence via the graph Laplacian
Ant colony and particle swarm optimisation
Stigmergy, self-organisation and agent-based modelling
Opinion dynamics and the wisdom of crowds: DeGroot model, voter model and epidemic spread on networks
Agent-based simulation of a market of traders or minibus routes

syllabus.title: Evaluation, ethics and research project
topics: Designing a multi-agent system for a real problem: mobile-money fraud, traffic or irrigation
Evaluating multi-agent systems: welfare, exploitability and robustness
Ethics and safety of multi-agent AI, including collusion in algorithmic pricing
Reading and critiquing recent papers; open problems

courses.title: Nonlinear and Optimal Control
topics: Lyapunov stability
Feedback linearisation
Linear quadratic regulation
Model predictive control
Trajectory optimisation
Dynamic programming
Control through contact
courses.description: Control of nonlinear dynamical systems and optimal control at graduate depth: phase-plane analysis, Lyapunov stability, feedback linearisation, linear quadratic regulation, model predictive control, trajectory optimisation, dynamic programming and control through contact. Students derive controllers on paper, then simulate and compare them on pendulums, cart-poles, drones and walking models in the maths lab and code runner.
modelledOn: Khalil, Nonlinear Systems
Tedrake, Underactuated Robotics: Algorithms for Walking, Running, Swimming, Flying, and Manipulation
Rawlings, Mayne and Diehl, Model Predictive Control: Theory, Computation, and Design
outcomes: Linearise nonlinear models, draw phase portraits and classify equilibria and limit cycles.
Prove stability of an equilibrium with a Lyapunov function and estimate its region of attraction.
Design feedback-linearising, backstepping and sliding-mode controllers for low-order nonlinear plants.
Derive and tune linear quadratic regulators and Kalman filters, and extend them to trajectory tracking.
Formulate and solve model predictive control and trajectory optimisation problems with constraints.
Apply dynamic programming to compute optimal policies and explain its limits and links to reinforcement learning.

syllabus.title: Nonlinear systems and the phase plane
topics: State-space models, equilibria, linearisation and the Jacobian
Phase portraits: nodes, saddles, foci, centres and limit cycles; Poincare-Bendixson theorem
Canonical examples: pendulum, cart-pole, Van der Pol oscillator and a planar quadrotor
Existence and uniqueness, Lipschitz conditions and finite escape time
Bifurcations and chaos: pitchfork and Hopf bifurcations, the Lorenz system

syllabus.title: Lyapunov stability
topics: Stability definitions: stable, asymptotically stable, exponentially stable, global
Lyapunov direct method: positive definite functions and the derivative along trajectories
LaSalle invariance principle
Linear systems: the Lyapunov equation and converse theorems
Region of attraction estimates and sum-of-squares certificates
Control Lyapunov functions and constructive stabilising feedback

syllabus.title: Feedback linearisation and nonlinear design
topics: Input-state linearisation: Lie derivatives, relative degree and the controllability conditions
Input-output linearisation, zero dynamics and minimum phase systems
Backstepping for strict-feedback systems
Sliding mode control: sliding surface, reaching condition and chattering reduction
Passivity and energy shaping: swing-up of a pendulum
Computed-torque control of robot manipulators and robustness to model error

syllabus.title: Linear quadratic optimal control
topics: The optimal control problem, cost functionals and the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation
Linear quadratic regulator: Riccati equation, infinite-horizon gain and guaranteed margins
Kalman filter, LQG and the separation principle
Weight tuning, integral action and tracking with LQR
Time-varying LQR, linearisation about a trajectory and iterative LQR

syllabus.title: Model predictive control
topics: Receding-horizon formulation with state and input constraints
Linear MPC as a quadratic program; terminal cost and sets; recursive feasibility and stability
Nonlinear MPC: sequential quadratic programming and real-time iteration
Tuning: horizon length, soft constraints, disturbance models and offset-free tracking
Applications: quadrotor tracking, a solar-battery microgrid for a Ghanaian clinic, and irrigation scheduling

syllabus.title: Trajectory optimisation
topics: Calculus of variations and Pontryagin minimum principle
Direct methods: single and multiple shooting, direct collocation and transcription to a nonlinear program
Differential flatness and minimum-snap trajectories
Sequential convex programming and differential dynamic programming
Time-optimal control: bang-bang solutions and switching curves

syllabus.title: Dynamic programming and learning
topics: Principle of optimality, the Bellman equation and value iteration on a grid
Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation and the curse of dimensionality
Approximate dynamic programming: policy iteration and function approximation
Links to reinforcement learning: policy gradient and actor-critic; safety concerns
Stochastic optimal control and Markov decision processes

syllabus.title: Control through contact
topics: Hybrid dynamics: impacts, Coulomb friction, stick-slip and complementarity conditions
Walking as a hybrid limit cycle: passive walkers, Poincare maps and stability of gaits
Contact-implicit trajectory optimisation
Hybrid MPC and mode scheduling; grasping and pushing with contact
Contact models: rigid versus compliant, and the simulation-to-reality gap

syllabus.title: Design project and comparison
topics: Choosing a plant, deriving its model and stating performance and constraint requirements
Controller comparison: feedback linearisation, LQR and MPC under disturbance, delay and model error
Robustness evaluation with Monte Carlo parameter variation
Technical report: results, limits, and what would be needed for hardware implementation

courses.title: Performance Modelling and Queueing Systems
topics: Markov chains and birth-death processes
M/M/1 and M/M/c queues
queueing networks and bottleneck analysis
workload characterisation
simulation of systems
capacity planning
measurement and confidence intervals
courses.description: The mathematics and measurement practice of predicting how computer and communication systems behave under load. Students derive Markov chain and queueing results, run discrete-event simulations and use the models to size systems such as call centres, cell sites, web services and mobile-money platforms.
modelledOn: Harchol-Balter, Performance Modeling and Design of Computer Systems
Lazowska, Zahorjan, Graham and Sevcik, Quantitative System Performance
Jain, The Art of Computer Systems Performance Analysis
Kleinrock, Queueing Systems, Volume 1: Theory
outcomes: Apply operational laws and bottleneck analysis to bound the throughput and response time of a system.
Model systems as Markov chains and birth-death processes and solve for steady-state distributions.
Derive and apply M/M/1, M/M/c, Erlang B and C and M/G/1 results to staffing and dimensioning problems.
Analyse open and closed queueing networks with product-form solutions and mean value analysis.
Characterise workloads from traces and build discrete-event simulations with valid statistical output analysis.
Produce a capacity plan that forecasts demand, validates a model against measurements and states cost and risk.

syllabus.title: Performance fundamentals and operational laws
topics: Metrics: throughput, latency, utilisation, response time and tail percentiles
Operational laws: utilisation law, Little's law, forced flow law and the interactive response time law
Open and closed workloads, and the pitfalls of benchmarking
Bottleneck analysis and asymptotic bounds on throughput and response time

syllabus.title: Probability and Markov chains
topics: Exponential and Poisson processes: memorylessness, merging and splitting
Discrete-time Markov chains: classification of states, stationary distribution and ergodicity
Continuous-time Markov chains: generator matrix, balance equations and uniformisation
Birth-death processes and detailed balance
Renewal processes and the inspection paradox
Transient analysis with the matrix exponential

syllabus.title: Single-station queues
topics: The M/M/1 queue: derivation of L, Lq, W and Wq and the response-time distribution
M/M/c and the Erlang C formula for staffing agents, counters and clinics
Loss systems: M/M/c/c and the Erlang B formula for trunk and channel dimensioning
Finite buffers and finite populations: M/M/1/K and machine-repairman models
M/G/1 and the Pollaczek-Khinchine formula; the effect of service-time variability and priority queues
Heavy-tailed service times and the Kingman approximation for G/G/1

syllabus.title: Queueing networks
topics: Tandem queues and Burke's theorem
Open Jackson networks and product-form solutions
Closed networks: Gordon-Newell form and mean value analysis
Multiclass networks and approximate mean value analysis
Balanced job bounds and finding the bottleneck station
Applications: a multi-tier web service and a packet-switched network

syllabus.title: Workload characterisation
topics: Collecting and cleaning traces; clustering requests into workload classes
Distribution fitting: exponential, lognormal and Pareto by maximum likelihood, QQ plots and the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test
Burstiness and self-similarity; Markov-modulated arrival processes
Session and think-time models and generating synthetic workloads

syllabus.title: Simulation of systems
topics: Discrete-event simulation: event list, simulation clock and state updates
Random number and variate generation: inverse transform and acceptance-rejection
Simulating queues, verifying against M/M/1 theory and deleting the warm-up period
Variance reduction: common random numbers, antithetic variates and control variates
Rare-event simulation and importance sampling

syllabus.title: Measurement and statistical analysis
topics: Output analysis: independent replications, batch means and confidence intervals
Steady-state versus terminating simulations and detecting the initial transient
Comparing alternatives: paired comparisons, confidence intervals on differences and ranking
Experimental design: 2^k factorial and fractional factorial designs
Measuring real systems: load testing, percentile reporting and coordinated omission

syllabus.title: Capacity planning and reliability
topics: The capacity planning cycle: forecasting demand, modelling, validating and sizing
Cost-performance trade-offs in the cloud: autoscaling, reserved versus on-demand capacity
Network dimensioning: link sizing for rural cell sites with Erlang models
Case study: sizing a mobile-money platform for a month-end peak
Availability and reliability: queues with failures, service level objectives and error budgets
Project: model, measure and size a system end to end

courses.title: Privacy Engineering and Privacy-Enhancing Technologies
topics: Privacy threat modelling
Differential privacy
Anonymous communication
Secure multi-party computation basics
Federated learning and privacy
Privacy-preserving data release
Evaluating privacy guarantees
courses.description: Designing systems that collect and use personal data without exposing people, from threat modelling and anonymisation to differential privacy, anonymous communication, secure computation and private machine learning. In the lab students implement the techniques, attack them, and measure what privacy they actually deliver.
modelledOn: Dwork and Roth, The Algorithmic Foundations of Differential Privacy
Hoepman, Privacy Is Hard and Seven Other Myths (privacy design strategies)
Deng et al., a privacy threat analysis framework (LINDDUN)
Evans, Kolesnikov and Rosulek, A Pragmatic Introduction to Secure Multi-Party Computation
outcomes: Model privacy threats in a system using data flow diagrams, adversary models and a structured threat taxonomy.
Measure re-identification risk and apply k-anonymity and its refinements, and demonstrate their weaknesses.
Implement differential privacy mechanisms, track a privacy budget and explain the privacy-utility trade-off.
Explain and simulate anonymous communication, secret-sharing based computation and private set intersection.
Train models with federated learning and differential privacy, and attack them with membership inference.
Audit and compare privacy guarantees and choose a technology for a given use case with reasons.

syllabus.title: Privacy concepts, law and identifiability
topics: Privacy as contextual integrity and informational self-determination; taxonomy of privacy harms
Legal frameworks: Ghana's Data Protection Act, comparable African laws and the GDPR; lawful bases and data subject rights
Principles: purpose limitation, data minimisation, storage limitation and privacy by design
Direct and quasi-identifiers, linkage attacks and re-identification
Data protection impact assessments

syllabus.title: Privacy threat modelling
topics: LINDDUN threat categories: linkability, identifiability, detectability, disclosure, unawareness and non-compliance
Data flow diagrams, trust boundaries and adversary models (honest-but-curious, malicious, global passive)
Privacy risk assessment: likelihood, impact and prioritisation
Privacy design strategies and patterns: minimise, hide, separate, aggregate, inform, control
Worked threat model of a mobile-money or health application

syllabus.title: Anonymisation and privacy-preserving data release
topics: k-anonymity, l-diversity and t-closeness; generalisation, suppression and Mondrian partitioning
Attacks on anonymised data: homogeneity, background knowledge and composition
Pseudonymisation, tokenisation and the pitfalls of hashing identifiers
Synthetic data: generation methods and privacy leakage
Releasing statistics: cell suppression, query auditing and reconstruction attacks
Data sharing agreements, data trusts and secure research enclaves

syllabus.title: Differential privacy
topics: Definition: epsilon and delta, neighbouring datasets, sensitivity, post-processing and composition
Mechanisms: randomised response, Laplace, Gaussian and exponential mechanisms
Privacy budget accounting: basic and advanced composition, zero-concentrated and Renyi accounting
Local versus central models; frequency estimation under local privacy and the shuffle model
Differentially private learning: per-example clipping, noise multiplier and DP-SGD
Deployment practice: choosing epsilon, census and telemetry examples, and open-source libraries

syllabus.title: Anonymous communication
topics: Identifiers and metadata at the network layer; anonymity sets and entropy metrics
Mix networks, onion routing and hidden services; circuit construction
Crowds, DC-nets and message batching
Attacks: traffic correlation, website fingerprinting, intersection and Sybil attacks
Blind signatures, anonymous credentials and private information retrieval

syllabus.title: Secure multi-party computation basics
topics: Adversary models: semi-honest and malicious; ideal functionality and simulation
Secret sharing: additive and polynomial sharing; secure addition and multiplication with Beaver triples
Garbled circuits and oblivious transfer
Private set intersection and homomorphic encryption (Paillier and the idea of BFV and CKKS)
Trusted execution environments and confidential computing: assumptions and costs
Applications: cross-bank fraud analytics, private statistics and salary studies

syllabus.title: Federated learning and privacy
topics: Federated averaging, client sampling, non-identical data and communication cost
Attacks: gradient inversion, membership inference, model inversion and memorisation
Secure aggregation and differentially private federated learning
Machine unlearning and the right to erasure
Cross-device learning on phones with low connectivity and cross-silo learning among hospitals
Fairness versus privacy trade-offs

syllabus.title: Evaluating privacy guarantees
topics: Empirical privacy audits: membership inference, shadow models and auditing differential privacy
Risk and utility metrics: prosecutor and journalist risk, information loss and the privacy-utility frontier
Comparing guarantees: syntactic versus semantic privacy, assumptions and threat-model mapping
Implementation pitfalls: floating-point attacks on noise samplers and budget leaks
Red-teaming, bug bounties and certification of privacy claims
Transparency documents: privacy notices, model cards and impact reports

syllabus.title: Privacy engineering in practice
topics: The privacy engineering lifecycle from requirements to operations
Choosing a privacy-enhancing technology: a decision guide by data location, trust and accuracy needs
Cost, performance and governance of deploying privacy-enhancing technologies
Project: privacy architecture for a health or payments data product

courses.title: Probabilistic Graphical Models
topics: Directed and undirected models
Exact inference and belief propagation
Parameter estimation and EM
Variational inference
Sampling and MCMC
Structure learning and causality
Deep generative models
courses.description: Representation, inference and learning in directed and undirected probabilistic models, from Bayesian networks and hidden Markov models to variational inference, MCMC, causal graphs and deep generative models. Students derive the algorithms and then run them on small networks, sampling problems and real-style datasets in the lab.
modelledOn: Koller and Friedman, Probabilistic Graphical Models: Principles and Techniques
Bishop, Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning
Murphy, Probabilistic Machine Learning: Advanced Topics
Pearl, Causality
outcomes: Represent a domain as a Bayesian network or Markov random field and read its independence assumptions from the graph.
Run and analyse exact inference by variable elimination, belief propagation and the junction tree algorithm, including its complexity.
Derive and implement maximum likelihood, Bayesian and EM parameter learning for graphical models.
Derive the evidence lower bound and implement mean-field and stochastic variational inference.
Implement Metropolis-Hastings, Gibbs and Hamiltonian Monte Carlo and diagnose convergence.
Use causal graphs to decide what can be identified from observational data, and relate deep generative models to latent-variable inference.

syllabus.title: Directed and undirected models
topics: Probability review: joint, marginal and conditional distributions, Bayes' rule, independence and conditional independence
Bayesian networks: factorisation, conditional probability tables and plate notation
d-separation, Markov blankets, I-maps and I-equivalence
Markov random fields: Hammersley-Clifford theorem, cliques and log-linear models
Factor graphs and conversion between representations; Gaussian and conditional linear Gaussian models

syllabus.title: Temporal and structured models
topics: Hidden Markov models: forward, backward and Viterbi algorithms
Linear dynamical systems: the Kalman filter and smoother
Dynamic Bayesian networks and particle filtering
Conditional random fields for sequence labelling
Topic models: the latent Dirichlet allocation generative process

syllabus.title: Exact inference
topics: Variable elimination: elimination orderings, induced width and treewidth
Sum-product belief propagation on trees and message passing
The junction tree algorithm: moralisation, triangulation and clique trees
Max-product and MAP inference; graph cuts for binary MRFs
Complexity of inference: NP-hardness, loopy belief propagation and its convergence

syllabus.title: Parameter estimation and EM
topics: Maximum likelihood and Bayesian estimation for Bayesian networks: sufficient statistics and Dirichlet priors
Learning Markov random fields: the partition function, gradients and contrastive methods
Expectation-maximisation: derivation via the lower bound, Gaussian mixtures and convergence
EM for HMMs (Baum-Welch) and for missing data; identifiability and local optima
Learning conditional random fields and structured prediction

syllabus.title: Variational inference
topics: KL divergence, the evidence lower bound and exponential families
Mean-field approximation: coordinate ascent updates, illustrated on the Ising model
Loopy belief propagation as Bethe free energy minimisation; expectation propagation
Stochastic variational inference, the reparameterisation trick and black-box variational inference
Variational Bayes for Gaussian mixtures and latent Dirichlet allocation

syllabus.title: Sampling and Markov chain Monte Carlo
topics: Importance sampling, rejection sampling and effective sample size
Markov chains: stationary distributions, detailed balance and ergodicity
Metropolis-Hastings, Gibbs sampling, and blocked and collapsed Gibbs samplers
Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, NUTS and diagnostics such as R-hat, autocorrelation and trace plots
Sequential Monte Carlo and approximate Bayesian computation

syllabus.title: Structure learning and causality
topics: Score-based structure learning: BIC, K2 and greedy hill climbing
Constraint-based learning: the PC algorithm and conditional independence tests
Causal graphs: interventions, the do-operator, the backdoor criterion and adjustment
Structural causal models, counterfactuals, front-door adjustment and identifiability
Causal discovery from observational data, with applications to malaria and public health surveillance

syllabus.title: Deep generative models and probabilistic programming
topics: Variational autoencoders and amortised inference
Normalising flows and autoregressive models
Generative adversarial networks, energy-based models and restricted Boltzmann machines
Diffusion and score-based models as latent-variable models; links to variational inference
Probabilistic programming with PyMC or Stan-style languages, and the course project

courses.title: Procedural Content Generation and Player Modelling
topics: Constructive and grammar-based generation
Search-based and evolutionary content generation
Machine-learned generators
Evaluating generators and expressive range
Player modelling and telemetry
Dynamic difficulty and experience-driven generation
Mixed-initiative design tools
courses.description: How games generate levels, maps and challenges by algorithm and how they learn from the people who play them. Students build constructive, evolutionary and learned generators, measure their output, and fit player models that drive adaptive difficulty.
modelledOn: Shaker, Togelius and Nelson, Procedural Content Generation in Games
Yannakakis and Togelius, Artificial Intelligence and Games
Russell and Norvig, Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach (search and learning chapters)
Bishop, Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning (clustering and generative model chapters)
outcomes: Implement constructive generators using noise, cellular automata, grammars, BSP trees and tile-constraint methods.
Formulate content generation as a search problem and build an evolutionary generator with a justified fitness function.
Train a simple machine-learned level generator and explain what its latent space and training data limit.
Evaluate a generator with expressive range analysis, playability checks and diversity metrics.
Build player models from telemetry using clustering, prediction and skill rating, and discuss their ethical limits.
Design an adaptive difficulty loop and a mixed-initiative design tool and test them against a stated player experience goal.

syllabus.title: Constructive and grammar-based generation
topics: Taxonomy of generators: online versus offline, necessary versus optional content, controllability and determinism
Noise and terrain: value and gradient noise, fractal octaves and diamond-square
Cellular automata for caves and islands; smoothing rules and connectivity repair
Dungeon generation: BSP trees, rooms-and-corridors and graph-based layouts
L-systems and shape grammars for plants, buildings and quests
Markov chains and wave function collapse for tile-based levels

syllabus.title: Search-based and evolutionary content generation
topics: Genetic algorithms: representation, selection, crossover and mutation for levels
Fitness functions: direct, simulation-based and interactive evaluation
Novelty search, quality diversity and MAP-Elites
Constraint solving and answer set programming for design rules
Multi-objective search: Pareto fronts and the NSGA-II algorithm

syllabus.title: Machine-learned generators
topics: Learning from existing levels: encoding, training data and its limits
N-gram and recurrent models for sequences of tiles and rhythm
Autoencoders and generative adversarial networks; searching the latent space
Reinforcement learning as a level designer and large generative models for text and art assets
Data scarcity, copyright and bias in learned generators

syllabus.title: Evaluating generators and expressive range
topics: Expressive range analysis: metrics such as linearity, leniency and density, and 2D histograms
Playability and solvability checks with simulated agents and path search
Diversity and novelty: edit distance, feature distance and repetition detection
Human evaluation: surveys, rankings and blind comparison of generated and hand-made content
Failure modes: degenerate content, bias towards simple outputs and confirmation of metrics

syllabus.title: Player modelling and telemetry
topics: Player types and motivation taxonomies; model-based versus model-free approaches
Telemetry features and clustering players with k-means and hierarchical methods
Predicting churn, purchase and skill with logistic regression and decision trees
Skill rating systems: Elo-style updates, Glicko and matchmaking
Learning from play traces: behaviour cloning, procedural personas and privacy and ethics of modelling

syllabus.title: Dynamic difficulty and experience-driven generation
topics: Flow theory: matching challenge to skill and the limits of the flow channel
Rule-based and model-based dynamic difficulty adjustment; rubber-banding
The experience-driven PCG loop: model the player, generate, evaluate, adapt
Affect and preference learning from ranked pairs
Bandits for content selection; fairness, manipulation and transparency in adaptation

syllabus.title: Mixed-initiative design tools
topics: Co-creative design: suggestion, critique and variation in a designer's tool
Constraint-based editing and automatic repair of designer sketches
Interface design for control: sliders, examples and seeds
Evaluating tools with designers: task time, quality and creative ownership
Tools for small teams and low-resource studios; explainability of suggestions

syllabus.title: Applications and project
topics: Generating quests, stories and dialogue with grammars and planning
Generating music, textures and shaders procedurally
Evaluating at scale: simulation, A/B tests and regression tests for generators
Case study: a mobile roguelike or puzzle game with generated levels and adaptive difficulty
Project: build, evaluate and report a generator coupled to a player model

courses.title: Programming Language Theory and Verification
topics: Operational and denotational semantics
Lambda calculus and type systems
Polymorphism and type inference
Program logics and separation logic
Abstract interpretation
Proof assistants and verified software
Effect systems and concurrency models
courses.description: The mathematical foundations of programming languages and the methods used to prove programs correct: operational and denotational semantics, lambda calculus, type systems and inference, program logics, abstract interpretation, proof assistants and effects. In the lab students step through derivations and write small interpreters, type checkers, verifiers and analysers.
modelledOn: Pierce, Types and Programming Languages
Winskel, The Formal Semantics of Programming Languages
Pierce et al., Software Foundations
Nielson, Nielson and Hankin, Principles of Program Analysis
