Reduce lambda terms under different evaluation strategies and encode data and recursion in the lambda calculus.
State and prove type safety for a typed language, and implement type checking and type inference.
Specify and verify imperative and pointer programs with pre- and postconditions, invariants and separation logic.
Build a sound abstract interpreter and reason about its precision.
Explain how proof assistants, SMT solvers, effect systems and concurrency models support verified software.

syllabus.title: Syntax and semantics of programming languages
topics: Concrete and abstract syntax, binding and substitution
Small-step structural operational semantics of a simple imperative language
Big-step semantics and its equivalence with small-step
Denotational semantics: domains, continuous functions and the meaning of while as a fixed point
Induction principles: structural induction and rule induction
Program equivalence and contextual equivalence

syllabus.title: The lambda calculus
topics: Untyped lambda terms: free and bound variables, alpha equivalence, beta reduction
Evaluation strategies: call by value, call by name and normal order
Confluence and the diamond property
Church encodings of booleans, numbers and pairs; the fixed-point combinator
De Bruijn indices and writing an interpreter

syllabus.title: Simple type systems
topics: The simply typed lambda calculus: typing rules and derivations
Progress and preservation as type safety
Strong normalisation and what it costs
Products, sums, records and subtyping
Propositions as types and proofs as programs
A first look at dependent types

syllabus.title: Polymorphism and type inference
topics: System F and parametric polymorphism; free theorems
Let-polymorphism in ML-style languages
Unification and the principal type algorithm
Type classes and ad hoc polymorphism
Bidirectional type checking

syllabus.title: Program logics and separation logic
topics: Pre- and postcondition triples for partial and total correctness
Weakest preconditions and verification condition generation
Loop invariants and termination measures
Soundness and relative completeness of the program logic
Separation logic: heaps, the separating conjunction and the frame rule
Verifying linked data structures with separation logic

syllabus.title: Abstract interpretation and static analysis
topics: Lattices, monotone functions, fixed points and Galois connections
Numerical abstract domains: signs and intervals
Widening and narrowing for fast convergence
Dataflow analysis as abstract interpretation
Soundness, precision and false alarms in practical analysers

syllabus.title: Proof assistants and verified software
topics: Interactive theorem proving: goals, tactics and proof terms
Inductive types and proofs about lists and trees
Verified software case studies: compilers, microkernels and file systems
SMT solvers and automated verification
Model checking and temporal properties

syllabus.title: Effects and concurrency
topics: Computational effects: state, exceptions and monads
Effect systems, algebraic effects and handlers
Concurrency models: shared memory, message passing and process calculi
Data races, linearizability and memory models
Ownership types and borrow checking; session types

syllabus.title: Research project
topics: Mechanising a type safety proof for a small language
Building a verified or well-tested interpreter
Reading and presenting a research paper in the field
Open problems: verification at scale and language design for safety

courses.title: Robot Learning
topics: Imitation learning
Policy gradient methods
Model-based reinforcement learning
Deep perception for manipulation
Sim-to-real transfer
Safe learning
Evaluation on real robots
courses.description: How robots acquire skills from demonstrations, rewards and models, and how those skills are made to work on real hardware safely. Students implement imitation, policy-gradient and model-based learning in small simulated tasks, train perception for grasping, test sim-to-real transfer, and evaluate policies with proper statistics.
modelledOn: Sutton and Barto, Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction
Siciliano and Khatib (eds.), Springer Handbook of Robotics
Kober, Bagnell and Peters, Reinforcement Learning in Robotics: A Survey
Published lecture notes and survey papers on deep reinforcement learning and imitation learning for robotics
outcomes: Formulate a robot task as a Markov decision process with states, actions, rewards and a data budget.

courses.title: Strategic Management of Information Technology

courses.title: Systems and Software Security

courses.description: A graduate course on securing the layers beneath applications: memory safety, isolation, privilege separation, program analysis, trusted hardware, operating system design and the software supply chain. Szekeres, Payer, Wei and Song, SoK: Eternal War in Memory
Saltzer and Schroeder, The Protection of Information in Computer Systems
NIST Secure Software Development Framework (SP 800-218) and the SLSA supply chain specification
outcomes: Explain and exploit classic memory corruption bugs in a controlled lab, and evaluate which mitigations stop them.
Design isolation and privilege separation for a service using processes, system call filters, namespaces and mandatory access control.
Find vulnerabilities with coverage-guided fuzzing, sanitizers, taint analysis and symbolic execution, and triage the results.
Describe how secure boot, measured boot and trusted execution environments establish trust, and their known attack classes.
Reason about secure operating system design, from the reference monitor to capability kernels and kernel hardening.
Assess and harden a software supply chain with provenance, signing, reproducible builds and pipeline controls.

syllabus.title: Security principles and threat models

Concolic execution and hybrid fuzzing

courses.description: A doctoral research seminar on sequential decision making when outcomes and observations are uncertain, from Markov decision processes and POMDPs to online planning, learned models and safety. Students read and critique recent papers, implement solvers, probe their limits experimentally, and write a research proposal.
modelledOn: Puterman, Markov Decision Processes: Discrete Stochastic Dynamic Programming
Kochenderfer, Wheeler and Wray, Algorithms for Decision Making
Sutton and Barto, Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction
Bertsekas, Dynamic Programming and Optimal Control
outcomes: Prove convergence properties of dynamic programming methods for MDPs and state their dependence on the discount factor.
Explain the computational hardness of partially observable and decentralised problems and compare exact, point-based and online solvers.
Implement and analyse sampling-based planners such as sparse sampling, UCT and belief-tree search.
Critique methods for hierarchical planning, learned models and model-based reinforcement learning, including their failure modes.
Formulate safety and risk requirements with constrained, robust and risk-sensitive objectives and verify them.
Write a research proposal that identifies an open problem, a benchmark and an evaluation plan.

syllabus.title: Markov decision processes

Value iteration and policy iteration; the contraction mapping argument
Linear programming formulation and its dual
Discounted, average-reward and stochastic shortest path criteria
Approximate dynamic programming and error bounds with function approximation
Seminar: reading classic and recent convergence results

syllabus.title: Partially observable models

Exact solution with alpha vectors and the complexity of POMDPs

Decentralised POMDPs and multi-agent decision problems
Belief representations: particles, predictive states and recurrent policies

syllabus.title: Online and Monte Carlo planning

UCT and regret analysis of Monte Carlo tree search
POMCP, DESPOT and belief-tree search
Continuous spaces: progressive widening and continuous-action search
Anytime and receding-horizon planning under real-time limits

syllabus.title: Hierarchical and temporal planning
topics: Options and semi-Markov decision processes
MAXQ and task hierarchies
Temporal logic specifications and product MDPs
Temporal planning with durative actions and concurrency
Skill discovery and abstraction

syllabus.title: Planning with learned models
topics: Model-based reinforcement learning: Dyna and ensemble models

Offline reinforcement learning and pessimism

syllabus.title: Safe and risk-sensitive decisions
topics: Constrained MDPs and Lagrangian methods

syllabus.title: Research proposal

courses.title: Provable Security and Cryptographic Protocols
topics: Security definitions and reductions
One-way functions and pseudorandomness
Commitments and zero-knowledge proofs
Secure multi-party computation
Lattice-based cryptography
Cryptanalysis case studies
Post-quantum transitions
courses.description: A doctoral research seminar on the foundations of modern cryptography: security definitions and reductions, pseudorandomness, zero-knowledge proofs, secure multi-party computation, lattice-based schemes, cryptanalysis and the move to post-quantum cryptography. Students read and critique recent papers, work through proofs and toy implementations in the maths lab, and prepare a research proposal with an artefact.
modelledOn: Katz and Lindell, Introduction to Modern Cryptography
Boneh and Shoup, A Graduate Course in Applied Cryptography
Peikert, A Decade of Lattice Cryptography
NIST post-quantum cryptography standardisation reports and draft standards
outcomes: State and compare security definitions for encryption, signatures and protocols, and write a reduction-based proof of a simple scheme.
Construct pseudorandom objects from one-way functions and explain the assumptions each construction needs.
Design and analyse commitments, sigma protocols and zero-knowledge proofs, including simulators, extractors and the removal of interaction.
Describe secure multi-party computation protocols for semi-honest and malicious adversaries and estimate their costs.
Explain how lattice problems yield encryption and signatures, and estimate concrete security with attack cost models.
Critique a published proof or attack, assess migration to post-quantum schemes, and defend a research proposal with an artefact.

syllabus.title: Security definitions and reductions
topics: Computational security: negligible functions, probabilistic polynomial-time adversaries, asymptotic versus concrete security
Game-based definitions (IND-CPA, IND-CCA, EUF-CMA) and simulation-based definitions
Proofs by reduction and hybrid arguments; tightness and security loss
Idealised models: the random oracle, ideal cipher and generic group, and critiques of them
Critiquing a proof: common errors in published security arguments

syllabus.title: One-way functions and pseudorandomness
topics: One-way functions, permutations and hard-core predicates
Pseudorandom generators from one-way functions and the length-extension argument
Pseudorandom functions from generators by a tree construction; Feistel networks and pseudorandom permutations
Message authentication and authenticated encryption; composition results
Number-theoretic assumptions (discrete log, CDH, DDH, RSA, factoring) and the five worlds of average-case complexity
Collision-resistant hashing: iterated and sponge constructions, and indifferentiability

syllabus.title: Commitments and zero-knowledge proofs
topics: Commitment schemes: hiding and binding, discrete-log-based and hash-based commitments
Interactive proofs: completeness and soundness; sigma protocols for discrete logarithm knowledge
Zero knowledge: simulators, honest-verifier versus malicious verifier, proofs of knowledge and extractors
Removing interaction by hashing the challenge; security in the random oracle model and known pitfalls
Succinct arguments: arithmetisation, polynomial commitments, trusted setup versus transparent proofs
Applications: anonymous credentials, private payments and verifiable computation

syllabus.title: Secure multi-party computation
topics: Adversary models: semi-honest and malicious; composition and the universal composability framework
Oblivious transfer and garbled circuits
Polynomial secret sharing and honest-majority protocols for arithmetic and Boolean circuits
Malicious security: cut-and-choose, authenticated sharing and zero-knowledge compilers
Threshold cryptography and links to homomorphic encryption
Applications and costs: private set intersection, auctions and joint statistics across hospitals

syllabus.title: Lattice-based cryptography
topics: Lattices, shortest and closest vector problems, and the basis reduction algorithm LLL
LWE and SIS; worst-case to average-case reductions; ring and module variants
Public-key encryption and key encapsulation from LWE: correctness and noise analysis
Lattice signatures: hash-and-sign and Fiat-style signing with aborts
Fully homomorphic encryption: noise growth and bootstrapping
Concrete security: BKZ cost models, lattice estimators and parameter selection

syllabus.title: Cryptanalysis case studies
topics: Generic attacks: birthday and meet-in-the-middle; differential and linear cryptanalysis
Implementation attacks: timing, cache, fault injection and padding oracles
Breaking deployed systems: weak randomness, nonce reuse in signatures and lattice small-root attacks on RSA
Break of a proposed post-quantum scheme: causes and lessons for scheme evaluation

syllabus.title: Post-quantum transitions
topics: Quantum attacks: period finding against factoring and discrete log, quantum search against symmetric keys, and resource estimates
Standardisation of post-quantum schemes: lattice, hash-based, code-based and multivariate families and their status
Hybrid constructions, crypto-agility and the harvest-now-decrypt-later threat
Migration in African contexts: constrained devices, bandwidth limits and national identity and payment systems

syllabus.title: Research seminar: proposal and artefact
topics: Surveying a topic and building a reading list
Formulating an open problem and a proof sketch
Building and testing a toy implementation or attack as an artefact
Presenting and defending the proposal

courses.title: Research Proposal and Grant Writing
topics: Framing a fundable research question
Literature synthesis and gap analysis
Specific aims and hypotheses
Methods, preliminary data and feasibility
Timelines, milestones and budgets
Mock review panel and peer critique
Data management plans and responsible research
courses.description: A doctoral seminar on turning a research idea into a fundable, defensible proposal: framing the question, synthesising literature, writing aims, planning methods and budgets, and surviving review. Candidates draft each section, plan the work in the diagram studio, and take part in mock panels run in the scenario engine.
modelledOn: Przeworski and Salomon, The Art of Writing Proposals
Booth, Colomb and Williams, The Craft of Research
Funder guidance for research grants and the FAIR data principles
outcomes: Frame a research problem as a significant, feasible and original question with a clear contribution.
Synthesise the literature into a gap analysis using a documented and reproducible search strategy.
Write specific aims and testable hypotheses with defined success criteria and contingency plans.
Justify methods, feasibility, timeline and budget in a form a review panel can score.
Critique a peer proposal using funder criteria, respond to critique, and prepare a data management and research ethics plan.

syllabus.title: Framing a fundable research question
topics: From topic to problem: significance, innovation and the contribution statement
Criteria for a good question: feasible, interesting, novel, ethical and relevant
Research paradigms in computing and health: design science, empirical, computational and mixed methods
Stakeholder needs and local relevance: problems that matter for health and biology in Africa
The one-page concept note and the two-minute pitch
The funder landscape: matching an idea to a programme

syllabus.title: Literature synthesis and gap analysis
topics: Search strategy: databases, keywords, Boolean queries and recording the search
Screening and selection: inclusion criteria and PRISMA-style flow diagrams
Critical appraisal of studies: bias, validity and strength of evidence
Synthesis matrices and thematic synthesis
Types of gap and positioning a contribution against prior work
Reference management, paraphrasing and citation practice

syllabus.title: Specific aims and hypotheses
topics: Anatomy of an aims page: problem, gap, objective, approach and impact
Testable hypotheses: null, alternative and falsifiability
Aim hierarchy, independence and contingencies
Expected outcomes, deliverables and success criteria
Revising aims through critique

syllabus.title: Methods, preliminary data and feasibility
topics: Choosing a study design: observational, experimental, computational and simulation
Data sources, sampling and power analysis
Computational methods: baselines, benchmarks, validation and error analysis
Preliminary data and pilot studies as evidence of feasibility
Risks, pitfalls and alternative approaches
Rigour, reproducibility and threats to validity

syllabus.title: Timelines, milestones and budgets
topics: Work breakdown, milestones and the critical path
Budget categories: personnel, equipment, cloud compute, data, travel and indirect costs
Budget justification narrative
Currency, inflation and funder rules in a cedi and dollar budget
Risk register and mitigation plan

syllabus.title: Writing for reviewers
topics: Narrative structure and plain, precise language
Abstracts, lay summaries and titles
Figures and visual abstracts that carry the argument
Reading funder guidelines and compliance checks
Responding to feedback and planning a resubmission

syllabus.title: Mock review panel and peer critique
topics: Reviewer roles and scoring criteria: significance, approach, innovation, investigator and environment
Scoring calibration and the pitfalls of reviewer bias
Writing a constructive written critique
Panel discussion and consensus ranking
Writing a rebuttal and a revised aims page
Preparing for an oral defence of the proposal

syllabus.title: Data management plans and responsible research
topics: Data management plans: types of data, storage, formats, metadata and FAIR sharing
Consent, sensitive health data and data protection requirements
Research integrity: authorship, conflicts of interest and misconduct
Open science, preregistration and community benefit-sharing
Final submission checklist and the oral pitch

courses.title: Statistical Learning Theory
topics: PAC learning and VC dimension
Rademacher complexity and generalisation bounds
Online learning and regret
Boosting and margin theory
Active and semi-supervised learning theory
Differential privacy
Theory of over-parameterised models
courses.description: A doctoral research seminar on why learning algorithms generalise: PAC and VC theory, Rademacher and PAC-Bayes bounds, online learning, boosting, active and semi-supervised learning, differential privacy and over-parameterised models. Students prove core results, test bounds numerically against simulated learners, critique recent papers and write a research proposal on an open problem.
modelledOn: Shalev-Shwartz and Ben-David, Understanding Machine Learning: From Theory to Algorithms
Mohri, Rostamizadeh and Talwalkar, Foundations of Machine Learning
Vershynin, High-Dimensional Probability
Dwork and Roth, The Algorithmic Foundations of Differential Privacy
outcomes: Prove sample-complexity and generalisation bounds using concentration inequalities, VC dimension and Rademacher complexity.
Analyse online learning algorithms through regret and mistake bounds, and relate online guarantees to statistical ones.
Explain boosting, active learning and semi-supervised learning through margin and label-complexity arguments.
Design and analyse differentially private learning mechanisms and quantify the accuracy cost of privacy.
Critique recent theoretical work on over-parameterised models, identifying which assumptions and bounds do and do not explain observed behaviour.
Formulate an open problem and write a research proposal with a precise question, related work, approach and evaluation plan.

syllabus.title: The learning problem and concentration
topics: Empirical risk minimisation, true risk, hypothesis classes and the realisable and agnostic settings
No-free-lunch theorem and the approximation-estimation trade-off
Concentration inequalities: Hoeffding, Bernstein and McDiarmid bounded differences
Uniform convergence for finite classes by the union bound
Surrogate losses and classification calibration
Bayes-optimal predictors and statistical consistency

syllabus.title: PAC learning and VC theory
topics: PAC and agnostic PAC learning; sample complexity definitions
Growth function, Sauer-Shelah lemma and VC dimension
Fundamental theorem of statistical learning: equivalence of learnability, uniform convergence and finite VC dimension
VC dimension of halfspaces, polynomial thresholds and neural networks
Lower bounds on sample complexity and the no-free-lunch argument
Computational complexity of learning: proper versus improper learning and hardness results

syllabus.title: Rademacher complexity and generalisation bounds
topics: Rademacher complexity, symmetrisation and generalisation bounds
Contraction lemma and bounds for linear classes with norm constraints
Margin bounds for support vector machines and kernel methods
Covering numbers, Dudley's entropy integral and chaining
Algorithmic stability and generalisation of regularised ERM
PAC-Bayes bounds and their use for non-vacuous bounds on learned models
Data-dependent and local complexity bounds; fast rates

syllabus.title: Online learning and regret
topics: The online protocol; mistake bounds, the Halving algorithm and Littlestone dimension
Perceptron mistake bound and online-to-batch conversion
Experts, weighted majority and Hedge
Online convex optimisation: online gradient descent and regret of order square root of T
Multi-armed and contextual bandits: UCB and EXP3
Adversarial versus stochastic settings; best-of-both-worlds algorithms

syllabus.title: Boosting and margin theory
topics: Weak learnability and the boosting question
AdaBoost: algorithm, training-error bound and the role of weak-learner edge
Margin explanation of generalisation and its criticisms
Boosting as coordinate descent and functional gradient descent; relation to support vector machines
Boosting under noise: convex and non-convex losses and robustness

syllabus.title: Active, semi-supervised and transfer learning theory
topics: Active learning: label complexity, disagreement coefficient and exponential savings
Query by committee and margin-based active learning
Semi-supervised learning: cluster and manifold assumptions, and when unlabelled data provably helps
Co-training and multi-view learning
Domain adaptation: discrepancy distances and generalisation bounds under shift
Learning with few labels in low-resource settings: transfer, weak supervision and what theory says about it

syllabus.title: Differential privacy
topics: Definition of pure and approximate differential privacy; post-processing and group privacy
Laplace, Gaussian and exponential mechanisms
Composition: basic and advanced composition, and privacy accounting
Private empirical risk minimisation and DP-SGD; the sample-complexity cost of privacy
Privacy and generalisation: adaptive data analysis and the reusable holdout
Privacy for health and mobile data: local differential privacy and federated analytics

syllabus.title: Theory of over-parameterised models
topics: Classical bias-variance versus double descent; interpolation and the failure of classical bounds
Benign overfitting in linear regression and minimum-norm interpolation
Implicit bias of gradient descent: convergence to the maximum-margin solution
Neural tangent kernel, lazy training and the limits of the kernel regime
Feature learning and mean-field analysis of two-layer networks
PAC-Bayes and compression-based bounds for deep networks
Limits of uniform convergence and stability explanations; open debates

syllabus.title: Research frontiers and proposal
topics: Reading a theory paper critically: assumptions, constants, tightness and empirical relevance
Scaling behaviour of generalisation and sample complexity in modern learning systems
Robust learning, calibration and uncertainty: theoretical guarantees and gaps
Open problems in the course and ways to formulate them as precise questions
Proposal workshop: structure, related work, preliminary results and evaluation plan
